e-12421.problem: Calculate the circulation $\Gamma$ of the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y,z) = y \,\mathbf{i} -x \,\mathbf{j} + z\,\mathbf{k}$ along the closed curve $C$ given by $\mathbf r(t) =  \sin (\pi t)\,\mathbf{i} + \cos (\pi t)\, \mathbf{j} + t(2-t)\,\mathbf{k}$ for $t \in [0,2].$
e-12421.worked_solution:
The circulation $\Gamma$ measures the total work done by a force $\mathbf F$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$
It is given by the formula

$$
\Gamma = \oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \textrm{d} \mathbf r
= \int_a^b \mathbf F(r(t)) \cdot \mathbf r'(t) \; \textrm{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x = \sin (\pi t), \qquad
y = \cos (\pi t), \qquad
z = t(2-t) = 2t-t^2.
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =y\,i-x\,j+z\,k \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,i-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,j+(2t-{t}^{2})\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $\mathbf r'(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t))\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t))\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t-{t}^{2})\,k \\  & =\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,i-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,j+2(1-t)\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,i-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,j+(2t-{t}^{2})\,k\,)\cdot (\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,i-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,j+2(1-t)\,k) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\cdot \pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)+(-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t))\cdot (-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t))+(2t-{t}^{2})\cdot 2(1-t) \\  & =\pi {cos}^{2}⁡(\pi t)+\pi {sin}^{2}⁡(\pi t)+2(2t-{t}^{2})(1-t) \\  & =\pi ({cos}^{2}⁡(\pi t)+{sin}^{2}⁡(\pi t))+2(2t-3{t}^{2}+{t}^{3}) \\  & =\pi +4t-6{t}^{2}+2{t}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{2}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\pi +4t-6{t}^{2}+2{t}^{3}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[\pi t+2{t}^{2}-2{t}^{3}+\frac{1}{2}{t}^{4}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =[2\pi +8-16+8]-[0] \\  & =2\pi \end{aligned}
$$

e-12435.knowledge_point: Evaluating a Surface Integral Using Stokes' Theorem
e-12435.problem:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by the closed curve $C$ with positive orientation and parametrization $\mathbf{r}(t) = (t^2-t^3)\,\mathbf{i} + (t^2-t) \, \mathbf{j} + (t^2-t)\,\mathbf{k}$ for $t \in [0,1).$
Given that $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z) = \mathbf{i} + x\, \mathbf{j} + y\,\mathbf{k},$ evaluate the integral

$$
\iint\limits_S \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}.
$$
e-12435.worked_solution:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
\oint\limits_{C} \mathbf{F}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}
= \iint\limits_S \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x = t^2-t^3, \qquad
y = t^2-t, \qquad
z = t^2-t.
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =i+x\,j+y\,k \\  & =i+({t}^{2}-{t}^{3})\,j+({t}^{2}-t)\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $\mathbf r'(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-{t}^{3})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-t)\,k \\  & =(2t-3{t}^{2})\,i+(2t-1)\,j+(2t-1)\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(i+({t}^{2}-{t}^{3})\,j+({t}^{2}-t)\,k)\cdot ((2t-3{t}^{2})\,i+(2t-1)\,j+(2t-1)\,k) \\  & =1\cdot (2t-3{t}^{2})+({t}^{2}-{t}^{3})\cdot (2t-1)+({t}^{2}-t)\cdot (2t-1) \\  & =2t-3{t}^{2}+(-{t}^{3}+2{t}^{2}-t)\cdot (2t-1) \\  & =2t-3{t}^{2}-2{t}^{4}+{t}^{3}+4{t}^{3}-2{t}^{2}-2{t}^{2}+t \\  & =3t-7{t}^{2}+5{t}^{3}-2{t}^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∮}_{C}F\cdot dr \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(3t-7{t}^{2}+5{t}^{3}-2{t}^{4})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[\frac{3}{2}{t}^{2}-\frac{7}{3}{t}^{3}+\frac{5}{4}{t}^{4}-\frac{2}{5}{t}^{5}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{3}{2}-\frac{7}{3}+\frac{5}{4}-\frac{2}{5} \\  & =\frac{1}{60}\end{aligned}
$$

e-12422.knowledge_point: Evaluating a Line Integral Using Stokes' Theorem
e-12422.problem:
Use Stokes' theorem to evaluate 

$$
\displaystyle{\oint\limits_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}},
$$

where $\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} = \langle -xz, \: -yz, \: x+z^2 \rangle,$ and $C$ is the intersection of the paraboloid $z=x^2+y^2$ and the plane $z=1.$ The curve $C$ is oriented counter-clockwise when viewed from above.
e-12422.worked_solution:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
\oint\limits_{C} \mathbf{F}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}
= \iint\limits_S \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}.
$$

There are many surfaces whose boundary is the curve $C$ representing the intersection of the paraboloid $z=x^2+y^2$ and the plane $z=1.$ One such surface would be the plane $S$ with the equation 

$$
z = g(x,y) = 1.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(1)=0 \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(1)=0\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into the expression for $\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F}{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\,F\,{|}_{z=g(x,y)} & =⟨-xz,\,-yz,\,{z}^{2}+x⟩{|}_{z=1} \\  & =⟨{{-x}_{⏟}}_{P},\,{{-y}_{⏟}}_{Q},\,{{1+x}_{⏟}}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-(-x)\cdot 0-(-y)\cdot 0+1+x)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(1+x)\,\text{d}A,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is region enclosed by the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane.

Now, note that the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane is the circle $x^2+y^2=1$ of radius $1$ centered at the origin. Therefore, using the change of variables to polar coordinates

$$
x = r \cos\theta, \qquad
y = r \sin\theta, \qquad
\textrm{d}A = r \, \textrm{d}r \textrm{d}\theta,
$$

 

we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(1+x)\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(1+r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\cdot r\,\text{d}\theta \,\text{d}r \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }r+{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta \,\text{d}r \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[r\theta +{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ]}_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}r \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}2\pi r\,\text{d}r \\  & =\pi [{r}^{2}]_{0}^{1} \\  & =\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Along the curve, F(r(t))=(0,-sin(t),cos(t)) and r'(t)=(cos(t),-sin(t),cos(t)). Their dot product is sin²(t)+cos²(t)=1, so Γ=∫₀^{2π}1 dt=2π.

after.problem: Calculate the circulation $Γ$ of the vector field $F(x,y,z)=-z\,j+y\,k$ along the closed curve $C$ given by $r(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,k$ for $t\in [0,2\pi ).$
after.worked_solution:
The circulation $Γ$ measures the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$
It is given by the formula

$$
Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,y=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,z=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =-z\,j+y\,k \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,k \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,k)\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,k) \\  & =0\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t+(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & ={sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t. \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }1\,\text{d}t \\  & =[t]_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =2\pi \end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

The circulation Γ measures the total work done by a force F in moving a particle along a closed curve C. It is given by the formula Γ=∮CF⋅dr=∫abF(r(t))⋅r′(t)dt.

Along the curve C, we have x=sin⁡t,y=cos⁡t,z=sin⁡t.

So,

F(r(t))=−zj+yk=−sin⁡tj+cos⁡tk.

Computing r′(t), we get

r′(t)=ddt(sin⁡t)i+ddt(cos⁡t)j+ddt(sin⁡t)k=cos⁡ti−sin⁡tj+cos⁡tk.

Therefore,

F(r(t))⋅r′(t)=(−sin⁡tj+cos⁡tk)⋅(cos⁡ti−sin⁡tj+cos⁡tk)=0⋅cos⁡t+(−sin⁡t)⋅(−sin⁡t)+cos⁡t⋅cos⁡t=sin2⁡t+cos2⁡t.=1.

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

Γ=∮CF⋅dr=∫02πF(r(t))⋅r′(t)dt=∫02π1dt=[t]02π=2π

Calculate the circulation Γ of the vector field F(x,y,z)=yi−xj+zk along the closed curve C given by r(t)=sin⁡(t)i+cos⁡(t)j+t2k for t∈[−π,π).

a
3π
b
5π
c
4π
d
2π
e
π
Submit

decision.explanation: F(r(t))=(cos(t),-sin(t),t²) and r'(t)=(cos(t),-sin(t),2t), so F(r(t))·r'(t)=1+2t³. Thus Γ=∫₋π^π(1+2t³) dt=2π, since the odd term integrates to zero.

after.name: Question 2
after.problem: Calculate the circulation $Γ$ of the vector field $F(x,y,z)=y\,i-x\,j+z\,k$ along the closed curve $C$ given by $r(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\,j+{t}^{2}\,k$ for $t\in [-\pi ,\pi ).$
after.worked_solution:
The circulation $Γ$ measures the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$
It is given by the formula

$$
Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\operatorname{sin}⁡(t),\,y=\operatorname{cos}⁡(t),\,z={t}^{2}.
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =y\,i-x\,j+z\,k \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\,i-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)\,j+{t}^{2}\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(t))\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(t))\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})\,k \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\,i-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)\,j+2t\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\,i-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)\,j+{t}^{2}\,k)\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\,i-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)\,j+2t\,k) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)+(-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t))\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t))+{t}^{2}\cdot 2t \\  & ={cos}^{2}⁡(\pi t)+{sin}^{2}⁡(t)+2{t}^{3} \\  & =1+2{t}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }(1+2{t}^{3})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[t+\frac{{t}^{4}}{2}]}_{-\pi }^{\pi } \\  & =((\pi -(-\pi ))+\frac{{\pi }^{4}-(-\pi )^{4}}{2}) \\  & =2\pi \end{aligned}
$$

a

b
5π
c
4π
d
2π
e

Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The circulation Γ measures the total work done by a force F in moving a particle along a closed curve C. It is given by the formula Γ=∮CF⋅dr=∫abF(r(t))⋅r′(t)dt.

Along the curve C, we have x=sin⁡(t),y=cos⁡(t),z=t2.

So,

F(r(t))=yi−xj+zk=cos⁡(t)i−sin⁡(t)j+t2k.

Computing r′(t), we get

r′(t)=ddt(sin⁡(t))i+ddt(cos⁡(t))j+ddt(t2)k=cos⁡(t)i−sin⁡(t)j+2tk.

Therefore,

F(r(t))⋅r′(t)=(cos⁡(t)i−sin⁡(t)j+t2k)⋅(cos⁡(t)i−sin⁡(t)j+2tk)=cos⁡(t)⋅cos⁡(t)+(−sin⁡(t))⋅(−sin⁡(t))+t2⋅2t=cos2⁡(πt)+sin2⁡(t)+2t3=1+2t3.

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

Γ=∮CF⋅dr=∫−ππF(r(t))⋅r′(t)dt=∫−ππ(1+2t3)dt=[t+t42]−ππ=((π−(−π))+π4−(−π)42)=2π

verification.explanation: Rechecking gives F(r(t))·r'(t)=cos²(t)+sin²(t)+2t³=1+2t³. Integrating from −π to π yields 2π because the cubic term is odd. The revealed solution confirms this; its cos²(πt) is a typographical error for cos²(t).

after.name: Question 3
after.problem: Calculate the circulation $Γ$ of the vector field $F(x,y,z)=y\,i-x\,j$ along the closed curve $C$ given by $r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,j+(1-{t}^{2})\,k$ for $t\in [-1,1).$
after.worked_solution:
The circulation $Γ$ measures the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$
It is given by the formula

$$
Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t),\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t),\,z=1-{t}^{2}.
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =y\,i-x\,j \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,i-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t))\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t))\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-{t}^{2})\,k \\  & =-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,i+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,j-2t\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,i-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,j)\cdot (-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,i+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,j-2t\,k) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\cdot (-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t))+(-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t))\cdot \pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)+0\cdot (-2t) \\  & =-\pi {sin}^{2}⁡(\pi t)-\pi {cos}^{2}⁡(\pi t) \\  & =-\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}(-\pi )\,\text{d}t \\  & =-\pi [t]_{-1}^{1} \\  & =-\pi (1-(-1)) \\  & =-2\pi \end{aligned}
$$

r′(t)=ddt(cos⁡(πt))i+ddt(sin⁡(πt))j+ddt(1−t2)k=−πsin⁡(πt)i+πcos⁡(πt)j−2tk.

Therefore,

F(r(t))⋅r′(t)=(sin⁡(πt)i−cos⁡(πt)j)⋅(−πsin⁡(πt)i+πcos⁡(πt)j−2tk)=sin⁡(πt)⋅(−πsin⁡(πt))+(−cos⁡(πt))⋅πcos⁡(πt)+0⋅(−2t)=−πsin2⁡(πt)−πcos2⁡(πt)=−π.

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

Γ=∮CF⋅dr=∫−11F(r(t))⋅r′(t)dt=∫−11(−π)dt=−π[t]−11=−π(1−(−1))=−2π

content.problem: Calculate the circulation $Γ$ of the vector field $F(x,y,z)=y\,i-x\,j$ along the closed curve $C$ given by $r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,j+(1-{t}^{2})\,k$ for $t\in [-1,1).$
content.worked_solution:
The circulation $Γ$ measures the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$
It is given by the formula

$$
Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t),\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t),\,z=1-{t}^{2}.
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =y\,i-x\,j \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,i-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t))\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t))\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-{t}^{2})\,k \\  & =-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,i+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,j-2t\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,i-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,j)\cdot (-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,i+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,j-2t\,k) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\cdot (-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t))+(-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t))\cdot \pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)+0\cdot (-2t) \\  & =-\pi {sin}^{2}⁡(\pi t)-\pi {cos}^{2}⁡(\pi t) \\  & =-\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}(-\pi )\,\text{d}t \\  & =-\pi [t]_{-1}^{1} \\  & =-\pi (1-(-1)) \\  & =-2\pi \end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 4
after.problem: Calculate the circulation $Γ$ of the vector field $F(x,y,z)=(x+y)\,i-z\,k$ along the closed curve $C$ given by $r(t)=(1-{t}^{2})\,i+{t}^{2}\,j+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,k$ for $t\in [-1,1).$
after.worked_solution:
The circulation $Γ$ measures the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$
It is given by the formula

$$
Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=1-{t}^{2},\,y={t}^{2},\,z=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t).
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =(x+y)\,i-z\,k \\  & =(1-{t}^{2}+{t}^{2})\,i-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,k \\  & =i-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-{t}^{2})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t))\,k \\  & =-2t\,i+2t\,j+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(i-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,k)\cdot (-2t\,i+2t\,j+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,k) \\  & =1\cdot (-2t)+0\cdot 2t+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\cdot \pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t) \\  & =-2t+\frac{\pi }{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi t).\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}(-2t+\frac{\pi }{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi t))\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[-{t}^{2}-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi t)}{4}]}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =(-1-\frac{1}{4})-(-1-\frac{1}{4}) \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 5
after.problem: Calculate the circulation $Γ$ of the vector field $F(x,y,z)=y\,i+x\,j$ along the closed curve $C$ given by $r(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,k$ for $t\in [0,2\pi ).$
after.worked_solution:
The circulation $Γ$ measures the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$
It is given by the formula

$$
Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,y=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,z=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =y\,i+x\,j \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,k \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j)\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,k) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+0\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & ={cos}^{2}⁡t-{sin}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }({cos}^{2}⁡t-{sin}^{2}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =[\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)}{2}]_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5
?

Calculate the circulation Γ of the vector field F(x,y,z)=yi+xj along the closed curve C given by r(t)=sin⁡ti+cos⁡tj+2sin⁡tk for t∈[0,2π).

a
0
b
π
c
4
d
2π
e
1
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The circulation Γ measures the total work done by a force F in moving a particle along a closed curve C. It is given by the formula Γ=∮CF⋅dr=∫abF(r(t))⋅r′(t)dt.

Along the curve C, we have x=sin⁡t,y=cos⁡t,z=2sin⁡t.

So,

F(r(t))=yi+xj=cos⁡ti+sin⁡tj.

Computing r′(t), we get

r′(t)=ddt(sin⁡t)i+ddt(cos⁡t)j+ddt(2sin⁡t)k=cos⁡ti−sin⁡tj+2cos⁡tk.

Therefore,

F(r(t))⋅r′(t)=(cos⁡ti+sin⁡tj)⋅(cos⁡ti−sin⁡tj+2cos⁡tk)=cos⁡t⋅cos⁡t+sin⁡t⋅(−sin⁡t)+0⋅2cos⁡t=cos2⁡t−sin2⁡t.

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

Γ=∮CF⋅dr=∫02πF(r(t))⋅r′(t)dt=∫02π(cos2⁡t−sin2⁡t)dt=∫02πcos⁡(2t)dt=[sin⁡(2t)2]02π=0

content.problem: Calculate the circulation $Γ$ of the vector field $F(x,y,z)=y\,i+x\,j$ along the closed curve $C$ given by $r(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,k$ for $t\in [0,2\pi ).$
content.worked_solution:
The circulation $Γ$ measures the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$
It is given by the formula

$$
Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,y=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,z=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =y\,i+x\,j \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,k \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j)\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,k) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+0\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & ={cos}^{2}⁡t-{sin}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }({cos}^{2}⁡t-{sin}^{2}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =[\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)}{2}]_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 6
after.problem:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by the closed curve $C$ with positive orientation and parametrization $r(t)=(2{t}^{3}-2t)\,i+(3{t}^{2}+3t)\,j+({t}^{3}-t)\,k$ for $t\in [-1,0).$
Given that $F(x,y,z)=z\,i+y\,k,$ evaluate the integral

$$
{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$
after.worked_solution:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=2{t}^{3}-2t,\,y=3{t}^{2}+3t,\,z={t}^{3}-t.
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =z\,i+x\,k \\  & =({t}^{3}-t)\,i+(3{t}^{2}+3t)\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{3}-2t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3{t}^{2}+3t)\,j-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}-t)\,k \\  & =(6{t}^{2}-2)\,i+(6t+3)\,j+(3{t}^{2}-1)\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(({t}^{3}-t)\,i+(3{t}^{2}+3t)\,k)\cdot ((6{t}^{2}-2)\,i+(6t+3)\,j+(3{t}^{2}-1)\,k) \\  & =({t}^{3}-t)\cdot (6{t}^{2}-2)+0\cdot (6t+3)+(3{t}^{2}+3t)\cdot (3{t}^{2}-1) \\  & =6{t}^{5}+9{t}^{4}+{t}^{3}-3{t}^{2}-t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∮}_{C}F\cdot dr \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}(6{t}^{5}+9{t}^{4}+{t}^{3}-3{t}^{2}-t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[{t}^{6}+\frac{9{t}^{5}}{5}+\frac{{t}^{4}}{4}-{t}^{3}-\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}]}_{-1}^{0} \\  & =0-(1-\frac{9}{5}+\frac{1}{4}+1-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{20}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∮}_{C}F\cdot dr \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}(6{t}^{5}+9{t}^{4}+{t}^{3}-3{t}^{2}-t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[{t}^{6}+\frac{9{t}^{5}}{5}+\frac{{t}^{4}}{4}-{t}^{3}-\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}]}_{-1}^{0} \\  & =0-(1-\frac{9}{5}+\frac{1}{4}+1-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{20}\end{aligned}
$$

after.problem:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by the closed curve $C$ with positive orientation and parametrization $r(t)=({t}^{2}+t)\,i+({t}^{3}+{t}^{2})\,j+(2{t}^{2}+2t)\,k$ for $t\in [-1,0).$
Given that $F(x,y,z)=y\,i+z\,j+x\,k,$ evaluate the integral

{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.

after.worked_solution:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x={t}^{2}+t,\,y={t}^{3}+{t}^{2},\,z=2{t}^{2}+2t.
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =y\,i+z\,j+x\,k \\  & =({t}^{3}+{t}^{2})\,i+(2{t}^{2}+2t)\,j+({t}^{2}+t)\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}+t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}+{t}^{2})\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{2}+2t)\,k \\  & =(2t+1)\,i+(3{t}^{2}+2t)\,j+(4t+2)\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(({t}^{3}+{t}^{2})\,i+(2{t}^{2}+2t)\,j+({t}^{2}+t)\,k)\cdot ((2t+1)\,i+(3{t}^{2}+2t)\,j+(4t+2)\,k) \\  & =({t}^{3}+{t}^{2})(2t+1)+(2{t}^{2}+2t)(3{t}^{2}+2t)+({t}^{2}+t)(4t+2) \\  & =2t+11{t}^{2}+17{t}^{3}+8{t}^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∮}_{C}F\cdot dr \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}(2t+11{t}^{2}+17{t}^{3}+8{t}^{4})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[{t}^{2}+\frac{11}{3}{t}^{3}+\frac{17}{4}{t}^{4}+\frac{8}{5}{t}^{5}]}_{-1}^{0} \\  & =0-(1-\frac{11}{3}+\frac{17}{4}-\frac{8}{5}) \\  & =\frac{1}{60}\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: By Stokes' theorem, integrate F(r(t))·r'(t) from −1 to 1. Along C, z=2y, so e^(z−2y)=1. The dot product is −2πsin²(πt)−2πcos²(πt)+2πcos(πt)=−2π+2πcos(πt). Its integral is −4π.

after.name: Question 8
after.problem:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by the closed curve $C$ with positive orientation and parametrization $r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,j+2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,k$ for $t\in [-1,1).$
Given that $F(x,y,z)=2y\,i-2x\,j+{e}^{z-2y}\,k,$ evaluate the integral

$$
{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$
after.worked_solution:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t),\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t),\,z=2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t).
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =2y\,i-2x\,j+{e}^{z-2y}\,k \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,i-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,j+{e}^{2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)}\,k \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,i-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,j+k.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t))\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t))\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t))\,k \\  & =-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,i+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,j+2\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,i-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,j+k)\cdot (-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,i+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,j+2\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,k) \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\cdot (-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t))-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\cdot \pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)+1\cdot 2\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t) \\  & =-2\pi {sin}^{2}⁡(\pi t)-2\pi {cos}^{2}⁡(\pi t)+2\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t) \\  & =-2\pi +2\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∮}_{C}F\cdot dr \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}(-2\pi +2\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t))\,\text{d}t \\  & =[-2\pi t+2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)]_{-1}^{1} \\  & =(-2\pi (1)+0)-(-2\pi (-1)+0) \\  & =-4\pi \end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

Let S be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary C with positive orientation. If a vector field F has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains S, then Stokes' theorem states that

∮CF⋅dr=∬ScurlF⋅dS.

Along the curve C, we have x=cos⁡(πt),y=sin⁡(πt),z=2sin⁡(πt).

So,

F(r(t))=2yi−2xj+ez−2yk=2sin⁡(πt)i−2cos⁡(πt)j+e2sin⁡(πt)−2sin⁡(πt)k=2sin⁡(πt)i−2cos⁡(πt)j+k.

Computing r′(t), we get

r′(t)=ddt(cos⁡(πt))i+ddt(sin⁡(πt))j+ddt(2sin⁡(πt))k=−πsin⁡(πt)i+πcos⁡(πt)j+2πcos⁡(πt)k.

Therefore,

F(r(t))⋅r′(t)=(2sin⁡(πt)i−2cos⁡(πt)j+k)⋅(−πsin⁡(πt)i+πcos⁡(πt)j+2πcos⁡(πt)k)=2sin⁡(πt)⋅(−πsin⁡(πt))−2cos⁡(πt)⋅πcos⁡(πt)+1⋅2πcos⁡(πt)=−2πsin2⁡(πt)−2πcos2⁡(πt)+2πcos⁡(πt)=−2π+2πcos⁡(πt).

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

∬ScurlF⋅dS=∮CF⋅dr=∫−11F(r(t))⋅r′(t)dt=∫−11(−2π+2πcos⁡(πt))dt=[−2πt+2sin⁡(πt)]−11=(−2π(1)+0)−(−2π(−1)+0)=−4π

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t),\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t),\,z=2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t).
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =2y\,i-2x\,j+{e}^{z-2y}\,k \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,i-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,j+{e}^{2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)}\,k \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,i-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,j+k.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t))\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t))\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t))\,k \\  & =-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,i+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,j+2\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,i-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,j+k)\cdot (-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,i+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,j+2\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,k) \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\cdot (-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t))-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\cdot \pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)+1\cdot 2\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t) \\  & =-2\pi {sin}^{2}⁡(\pi t)-2\pi {cos}^{2}⁡(\pi t)+2\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t) \\  & =-2\pi +2\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t).\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∮}_{C}F\cdot dr \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}(-2\pi +2\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t))\,\text{d}t \\  & =[-2\pi t+2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)]_{-1}^{1} \\  & =(-2\pi (1)+0)-(-2\pi (-1)+0) \\  & =-4\pi \end{aligned}

after.worked_solution:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x={t}^{3}-t,\,y=2{t}^{2}+1,\,z={t}^{2}-1.
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =y\,i+3\,j+yz\,k \\  & =(2{t}^{2}+1)\,i+3\,j+(2{t}^{2}+1)({t}^{2}-1)\,k \\  & =(2{t}^{2}+1)\,i+3\,j+(2{t}^{4}-{t}^{2}-1)\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}-t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{2}+1)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-1)\,k \\  & =(3{t}^{2}-1)\,i+4t\,j+2t\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =((2{t}^{2}+1)\,i+3\,j+(2{t}^{4}-{t}^{2}-1)\,k)\cdot ((3{t}^{2}-1)\,i+4t\,j+2t\,k) \\  & =(2{t}^{2}+1)(3{t}^{2}-1)+3(4t)+(2{t}^{4}-{t}^{2}-1)(2t) \\  & =-1+10t+{t}^{2}-2{t}^{3}+6{t}^{4}+4{t}^{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

Computing r′(t), we get r′(t)=ddt(t3−t)i+ddt(2t2+1)j+ddt(t2−1)k=(3t2−1)i+4tj+2tk.

content.knowledge_point: Evaluating a Surface Integral Using Stokes' Theorem
content.problem:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by the closed curve $C$ with positive orientation and parametrization $r(t)=({t}^{3}-t)\,i+(2{t}^{2}+1)\,j+({t}^{2}-1)\,k$ for $t\in [-1,1).$
Given that $F(x,y,z)=y\,i+3\,j+yz\,k,$ evaluate the integral

$$
{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$
content.worked_solution:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x={t}^{3}-t,\,y=2{t}^{2}+1,\,z={t}^{2}-1.
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =y\,i+3\,j+yz\,k \\  & =(2{t}^{2}+1)\,i+3\,j+(2{t}^{2}+1)({t}^{2}-1)\,k \\  & =(2{t}^{2}+1)\,i+3\,j+(2{t}^{4}-{t}^{2}-1)\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}-t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{2}+1)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-1)\,k \\  & =(3{t}^{2}-1)\,i+4t\,j+2t\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =((2{t}^{2}+1)\,i+3\,j+(2{t}^{4}-{t}^{2}-1)\,k)\cdot ((3{t}^{2}-1)\,i+4t\,j+2t\,k) \\  & =(2{t}^{2}+1)(3{t}^{2}-1)+3(4t)+(2{t}^{4}-{t}^{2}-1)(2t) \\  & =-1+10t+{t}^{2}-2{t}^{3}+6{t}^{4}+4{t}^{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∮}_{C}F\cdot dr \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}(-1+10t+{t}^{2}-2{t}^{3}+6{t}^{4}+4{t}^{5})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[-t+5{t}^{2}+\frac{1}{3}{t}^{3}-\frac{1}{2}{t}^{4}+\frac{6}{5}{t}^{5}+\frac{2}{3}{t}^{6}]}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =(-1+5+\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{2}+\frac{6}{5}+\frac{2}{3})-(1+5-\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{2}-\frac{6}{5}+\frac{2}{3}) \\  & =-2+\frac{2}{3}+\frac{12}{5} \\  & =\frac{16}{15}\end{aligned}
$$

after.problem:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by the closed curve $C$ with positive orientation and parametrization $r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,j+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,k$ for $t\in [-1,1).$
Given that $F(x,y,z)=y\,i+x\,k,$ evaluate the integral

$$
{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$
after.worked_solution:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t),\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t),\,z=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t).
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =y\,i+x\,k \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t))\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t))\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t))\,k \\  & =-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,i+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,j-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,k)\cdot (-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,i+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,j-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,k) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\cdot (-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t))+0\cdot \pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\cdot (-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)) \\  & =-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)-\pi {sin}^{2}⁡(\pi t).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∮}_{C}F\cdot dr \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}(-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)-\pi {sin}^{2}⁡(\pi t))\,\text{d}t \\  & =-{\int }_{-1}^{1}(\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)+\frac{\pi }{2}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi t)))\,\text{d}t \\  & =-{[\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡(\pi t)}{2}+\frac{\pi t}{2}-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi t)}{4}]}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =-[0+\frac{\pi }{2}+0-(0-\frac{\pi }{2}+0)] \\  & =-\pi \end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Evaluating a Surface Integral Using Stokes' Theorem
content.problem:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by the closed curve $C$ with positive orientation and parametrization $r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,j+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,k$ for $t\in [-1,1).$
Given that $F(x,y,z)=y\,i+x\,k,$ evaluate the integral

$$
{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$
content.worked_solution:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t),\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t),\,z=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t).
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =y\,i+x\,k \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t))\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t))\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t))\,k \\  & =-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,i+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,j-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,k)\cdot (-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,i+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,j-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,k) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\cdot (-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t))+0\cdot \pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\cdot (-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)) \\  & =-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)-\pi {sin}^{2}⁡(\pi t).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∮}_{C}F\cdot dr \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}(-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)-\pi {sin}^{2}⁡(\pi t))\,\text{d}t \\  & =-{\int }_{-1}^{1}(\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)+\frac{\pi }{2}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi t)))\,\text{d}t \\  & =-{[\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡(\pi t)}{2}+\frac{\pi t}{2}-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi t)}{4}]}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =-[0+\frac{\pi }{2}+0-(0-\frac{\pi }{2}+0)] \\  & =-\pi \end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Counter-clockwise orientation viewed from above requires the upward surface element (−2x,−4y,1) dx dy. Its dot product with curl F=(y,−x,1) is 2xy+1. The projected triangle has 0≤x≤1 and x−1≤y≤0, giving option e.

after.worked_solution:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

There are many surfaces whose boundary is the curve $C$ representing the intersection of the paraboloid $z=1+{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}$ and the boundary of our infinite vertical column. One such surface is our paraboloid $S$ with the equation 

$$
z=g(x,y)=1+{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(1+{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2})=2x \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(1+{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2})=4y\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into expression for $\text{curl}\,F:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\,F\,{|}_{z=g(x,y)} & =⟨y,\,-x,\,1⟩{|}_{z=1+{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}} \\  & =⟨y,\,-x,\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨{{y}_{⏟}}_{P},\,{{-x}_{⏟}}_{Q},\,{{1}_{⏟}}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-y\cdot (2x)-(-x)\cdot (4y)+1)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2xy+1)\,\text{d}A,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is region enclosed by the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane, shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14071512/assets/d84b3ecc79c58a128d2f7ea262692d9f66dd9882ff244fb7c3dadd2b2571b550.png)

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(2xy+1)\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{x-1}^{0}\,2xy+1\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Let C be the intersection of the paraboloid z=1+x2+2y2 and the boundary of the infinite vertical column enclosed by the planes x−y=1, x=0, and y=0. Given that the curve C is oriented counter-clockwise when viewed from above and curlF=⟨y,−x,1⟩, the circulation of F along C can be written as ∮CF⋅dr=

a
∫01∫0x−1−2xy+1dydx
b
∫01∫0x−12xy+1dydx
c
∫01∫01−xx2+2y2dydx
d
∫01∫x−10−2xy−1dydx
e
∫01∫x−102xy+1dydx
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let S be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary C with positive orientation. If a vector field F has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains S, then Stokes' theorem states that

∮CF⋅dr=∬ScurlF⋅dS.

There are many surfaces whose boundary is the curve C representing the intersection of the paraboloid z=1+x2+2y2 and the boundary of our infinite vertical column. One such surface is our paraboloid S with the equation

z=g(x,y)=1+x2+2y2.

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph z=g(x,y):

∂g∂x=∂∂x(1+x2+2y2)=2x∂g∂y=∂∂y(1+x2+2y2)=4y

Next, we substitute the equation z=g(x,y) into expression for curlF:

curlF|z=g(x,y)=⟨y,−x,1⟩|z=1+x2+2y2=⟨y,−x,1⟩=⟨y⏟P,−x⏟Q,1⏟R⟩

So, we have

∬ScurlF⋅dS=∬D(−P∂g∂x−Q∂g∂y+R)dA=∬D(−y⋅(2x)−(−x)⋅(4y)+1)dA=∬D(2xy+1)dA,

where D is region enclosed by the projection of C onto the xy-plane, shown below.

Therefore, we obtain

∬D(2xy+1)dA=∫01∫x−102xy+1dydx.

Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

There are many surfaces whose boundary is the curve $C$ representing the intersection of the paraboloid $z=1+{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}$ and the boundary of our infinite vertical column. One such surface is our paraboloid $S$ with the equation 

$$
z=g(x,y)=1+{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(1+{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2})=2x \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(1+{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2})=4y\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into expression for $\text{curl}\,F:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\,F\,{|}_{z=g(x,y)} & =⟨y,\,-x,\,1⟩{|}_{z=1+{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}} \\  & =⟨y,\,-x,\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨{{y}_{⏟}}_{P},\,{{-x}_{⏟}}_{Q},\,{{1}_{⏟}}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-y\cdot (2x)-(-x)\cdot (4y)+1)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2xy+1)\,\text{d}A,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is region enclosed by the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane, shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14071512/assets/d84b3ecc79c58a128d2f7ea262692d9f66dd9882ff244fb7c3dadd2b2571b550.png)

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(2xy+1)\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{x-1}^{0}\,2xy+1\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Stokes' theorem uses the upward surface element (2x,2y,1) dx dy for the stated orientation. Dotting with curl F=(−2z,0,0) gives −4xz=4x³+4xy²−40x. The projected triangle has 0≤x≤1 and 0≤y≤1−x, so option e is correct.

after.worked_solution:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

There are many surfaces whose boundary is the curve $C$ representing the intersection of the paraboloid $z=10-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}$ and the boundary of our infinite vertical column. One such surface is our paraboloid $S$ with the equation 

$$
z=g(x,y)=10-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(10-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})=-2x \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(10-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})=-2y\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into expression for $\text{curl}\,F:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\,F\,{|}_{z=g(x,y)} & =⟨-2z,\,0,\,0⟩{|}_{z=10-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}} \\  & =⟨-2(10-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}),\,0,\,0⟩ \\  & =⟨{{2{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}-20}_{⏟}}_{P},\,{{0}_{⏟}}_{Q},\,{{0}_{⏟}}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-(2{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}-20)\cdot (-2x)-0\cdot (-2y)+0)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(4{x}^{3}+4x{y}^{2}-40x)\,\text{d}A,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is region enclosed by the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane, shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14071512/assets/c181e209cca01a1d6e372caa7f7810a5fa4aa9f177595bd92f937a7cba8b8a75.png)

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(4{x}^{3}+4x{y}^{2}-40x)\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1-x}\,4{x}^{3}+4x{y}^{2}-40x\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

∮CF⋅dr=∬ScurlF⋅dS.

There are many surfaces whose boundary is the curve C representing the intersection of the paraboloid z=10−x2−y2 and the boundary of our infinite vertical column. One such surface is our paraboloid S with the equation

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph z=g(x,y):

∂g∂x=∂∂x(10−x2−y2)=−2x∂g∂y=∂∂y(10−x2−y2)=−2y

Next, we substitute the equation z=g(x,y) into expression for curlF:

where D is region enclosed by the projection of C onto the xy-plane, shown below.

content.worked_solution:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

There are many surfaces whose boundary is the curve $C$ representing the intersection of the paraboloid $z=10-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}$ and the boundary of our infinite vertical column. One such surface is our paraboloid $S$ with the equation 

$$
z=g(x,y)=10-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(10-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})=-2x \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(10-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})=-2y\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into expression for $\text{curl}\,F:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\,F\,{|}_{z=g(x,y)} & =⟨-2z,\,0,\,0⟩{|}_{z=10-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}} \\  & =⟨-2(10-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}),\,0,\,0⟩ \\  & =⟨{{2{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}-20}_{⏟}}_{P},\,{{0}_{⏟}}_{Q},\,{{0}_{⏟}}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-(2{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}-20)\cdot (-2x)-0\cdot (-2y)+0)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(4{x}^{3}+4x{y}^{2}-40x)\,\text{d}A,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is region enclosed by the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane, shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14071512/assets/c181e209cca01a1d6e372caa7f7810a5fa4aa9f177595bd92f937a7cba8b8a75.png)

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(4{x}^{3}+4x{y}^{2}-40x)\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1-x}\,4{x}^{3}+4x{y}^{2}-40x\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 13
after.problem:
Use Stokes' theorem to evaluate 

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr,
$$

where $\text{curl}\,F=⟨-x{e}^{z},\,0,\,{e}^{z}⟩,$ and $C$ is the intersection of the paraboloid $z={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}$ and the plane $z=4.$ The curve $C$ is oriented counter-clockwise when viewed from above.
after.worked_solution:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

There are many surfaces whose boundary is the curve $C$ representing the intersection of the paraboloid $z={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}$ and the plane $z=4.$ One such surface would be the plane $S$ with the equation 

$$
z=g(x,y)=4.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4)=0 \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4)=0\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into the expression for $\text{curl}\,F:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\,F\,{|}_{z=g(x,y)} & =⟨-x{e}^{z},\,0,\,{e}^{z}⟩{|}_{z=4} \\  & =⟨{{-x{e}^{4}}_{⏟}}_{P},\,{{0}_{⏟}}_{Q},\,{{{e}^{4}}_{⏟}}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-0\cdot (-x{e}^{4})-0\cdot 0+{e}^{4})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}{e}^{4}\,\text{d}A,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is region enclosed by the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane.

Notice that the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane is the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=4$ with radius $2$ centered at the origin. Therefore, using the change of variables to polar coordinates

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\text{d}A=r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta ,
$$

 

we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}{e}^{4}\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2}{e}^{4}\cdot r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={e}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta \cdot {\int }_{0}^{2}r\,\text{d}r \\  & ={e}^{4}[\theta ]_{\theta =0}^{\theta =2\pi }\cdot {[\frac{{r}^{2}}{2}]}_{r=0}^{r=2} \\  & ={e}^{4}(2\pi -0)\cdot (2-0) \\  & =4\pi {e}^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Let q=x²+y²+1. The upward surface element is (2x/q²,2y/q²,1) dx dy. Dotting with curl F=(x,y,−2/q) gives 2(x²+y²)/q²−2/q=−2/q². The projected region is [−1,1]×[−1,1], so Stokes' theorem gives option d.

after.worked_solution:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

There are many surfaces whose boundary is the curve $C$ representing the intersection of the surface $z=\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1}$ and the boundary of our infinite vertical column. One such surface is our surface $S$ with the equation 

$$
z=g(x,y)=\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1}.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1})=\frac{-2x}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)^{2}} \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1})=\frac{-2y}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into expression for $\text{curl}\,F:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\,F\,{|}_{z=g(x,y)} & =⟨x,\,y,\,-2z⟩{|}_{z=1/({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)} \\  & =⟨{{x}_{⏟}}_{P},\,{{y}_{⏟}}_{Q},\,{{-\frac{2}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1}}_{⏟}}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-x\cdot \frac{-2x}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)^{2}}-y\cdot \frac{-2y}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)^{2}}-\frac{2}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-\frac{2}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)^{2}}\,\text{d}A,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is region enclosed by the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane, shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14071512/assets/b215ec1e3330f96e7e606e085721b2dd1f50d113f0151e36ec98e6d0a6f54e73.png)

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}-\frac{2}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)^{2}}\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{-1}^{1}\,-\frac{2}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)^{2}}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 14

Let C be the intersection of the surface z=1x2+y2+1 and the boundary of the infinite vertical column enclosed by the planes x=±1, and y=±1. Given that the curve C is oriented counter-clockwise when viewed from above and curlF=⟨x,y,−2z⟩, the circulation of F along C can be written as ∮CF⋅dr=

a
∫−11∫−11−y2(x2+y2+1)2dydx
b
∫−11∫−11x2(x2+y2+1)2dydx
c
∫−11∫−11−4(x2+y2+1)2dydx
d
∫−11∫−11−2(x2+y2+1)2dydx
e
∫−11∫−11−xy(x2+y2+1)2dydx
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Let S be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary C with positive orientation. If a vector field F has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains S, then Stokes' theorem states that

content.worked_solution:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

There are many surfaces whose boundary is the curve $C$ representing the intersection of the surface $z=\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1}$ and the boundary of our infinite vertical column. One such surface is our surface $S$ with the equation 

$$
z=g(x,y)=\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1}.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1})=\frac{-2x}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)^{2}} \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1})=\frac{-2y}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into expression for $\text{curl}\,F:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\,F\,{|}_{z=g(x,y)} & =⟨x,\,y,\,-2z⟩{|}_{z=1/({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)} \\  & =⟨{{x}_{⏟}}_{P},\,{{y}_{⏟}}_{Q},\,{{-\frac{2}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1}}_{⏟}}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-x\cdot \frac{-2x}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)^{2}}-y\cdot \frac{-2y}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)^{2}}-\frac{2}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-\frac{2}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)^{2}}\,\text{d}A,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is region enclosed by the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane, shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14071512/assets/b215ec1e3330f96e7e606e085721b2dd1f50d113f0151e36ec98e6d0a6f54e73.png)

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}-\frac{2}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)^{2}}\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{-1}^{1}\,-\frac{2}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)^{2}}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$
